title: Grade 12 Physics — Alternating Current
description: AC circuits — Vrms, Irms, phasors, LCR circuits, resonance, power factor, transformers (CBSE Ch. 7)
subject: physics

questions.question: Alternating current (AC) differs from direct current (DC) in that AC:
options: Periodically reverses direction and changes magnitude sinusoidally
questions.explanation: AC periodically reverses direction (unlike DC which flows in one constant direction). Household electricity (50 Hz in India) changes direction 100 times per second. AC can be stepped up/down using transformers — making long-distance transmission efficient.

questions.question: The RMS (root mean square) voltage Vrms is related to the peak voltage V₀ by:
questions.explanation: Vrms = V₀/√2 ≈ 0.707 V₀. For a sinusoidal AC: Vrms is the equivalent DC voltage that produces the same power dissipation. India's household supply is 230 V RMS, meaning peak voltage ≈ 325 V.

questions.question: In a purely resistive AC circuit, the phase relationship between voltage V and current I is:
options: Voltage and current are in phase (φ = 0)
questions.explanation: In a pure resistor, V = IR (Ohm's law applies instantaneously). Both V and I follow the same sinusoidal pattern — they are perfectly in phase. Power = VrmsIrms (maximum, since cos φ = cos 0° = 1).

questions.question: In a purely inductive AC circuit, the current:
options: Is in phase with the voltage
questions.explanation: In a pure inductor, V = L dI/dt. The induced EMF opposes the change in current, causing current to lag the voltage by 90° (π/2 radians). Mnemonic: In an inductor, 'ELI' — E (voltage) leads I (current).

questions.question: In a purely capacitive AC circuit, the current:
options: Is in phase with the voltage
questions.explanation: In a pure capacitor, current flows as the capacitor charges/discharges. I = C dV/dt — current reaches its peak before voltage does. Current leads voltage by 90°. Mnemonic: 'ICE' — I (current) before E (voltage) in a Capacitor.

questions.question: Inductive reactance XL (the opposition offered by an inductor to AC) is given by:
questions.explanation: XL = ωL = 2πfL (unit: ohms, Ω). Inductive reactance increases with frequency — at very high frequencies, an inductor blocks AC completely. At f = 0 (DC), XL = 0 (inductor is just a wire for DC).

questions.question: Capacitive reactance XC (the opposition offered by a capacitor to AC) is given by:
questions.explanation: XC = 1/ωC = 1/(2πfC) (unit: ohms, Ω). Capacitive reactance decreases with increasing frequency — at very high frequencies, a capacitor passes AC easily. At f = 0 (DC), XC = ∞ (capacitor blocks DC completely).

questions.question: In a series LCR circuit, resonance occurs when:
options: XL = XC (inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance)
questions.explanation: At resonance, XL = XC. The net reactance is zero, impedance Z = R (minimum), and current amplitude is maximum (I = V/R). The circuit behaves as a pure resistor at the resonant frequency.

questions.question: The resonant frequency f₀ of a series LCR circuit is:
questions.explanation: At resonance: XL = XC → ωL = 1/ωC → ω² = 1/LC → ω₀ = 1/√(LC) → f₀ = ω₀/(2π) = 1/(2π√LC). This is the natural frequency of the LC circuit — at this frequency, energy oscillates between the inductor and capacitor.

questions.question: The power factor of an AC circuit is defined as cos φ, where φ is the phase angle. For a purely resistive circuit:
questions.explanation: In a purely resistive circuit, φ = 0°, so power factor = cos 0° = 1. This means all the electrical energy supplied is consumed as heat — maximum efficiency. For purely reactive circuits (inductor or capacitor), power factor = 0.

questions.question: The average power consumed in an AC circuit is:
questions.explanation: P = VrmsIrms cos φ. The cos φ factor (power factor) accounts for the phase difference between V and I. For purely reactive circuits (φ = 90°), cos φ = 0 and P = 0 — no net power is consumed (wattless current).

questions.question: Wattless current refers to the current component in an AC circuit that:
options: Is 90° out of phase with voltage — in a purely reactive circuit, no net energy is consumed
questions.explanation: In a purely reactive circuit (pure L or pure C), current and voltage are 90° out of phase. Power = VrmsIrms cos 90° = 0. Energy is alternately stored and returned — no net dissipation. This reactive current is called 'wattless current.'

questions.question: In a step-up transformer, compared to the primary coil:
options: The secondary has fewer turns and higher voltage
The secondary has more turns, higher voltage, and lower current
The secondary has more turns, lower voltage, and higher current
Both coils have the same number of turns
questions.explanation: Step-up transformer: Ns > Np → Vs > Vp (voltage increases). By energy conservation (assuming 100% efficiency): VpIp = VsIs → Is = Ip × Vp/Vs < Ip (current decreases). Step-up increases voltage, decreases current — used for long-distance power transmission.

questions.question: Transformers work on AC but NOT DC because:
options: DC has too high a frequency for transformers to handle
DC cannot flow through copper wires
Transformers work on electromagnetic induction — a changing flux is needed; DC produces constant flux (no EMF induced)
DC always exceeds the voltage rating of transformers
questions.explanation: Faraday's law: EMF = −N dΦ/dt. With AC, the magnetic flux changes continuously — inducing EMF in the secondary. With DC, flux is constant (dΦ/dt = 0), so no EMF is induced. Transformers need changing flux — hence AC only.

questions.question: The Q-factor (quality factor) of a series LCR circuit measures:
options: The ratio of resistance to impedance
The number of oscillations before energy runs out
The sharpness of resonance — a high Q means narrow bandwidth and selective tuning
questions.explanation: Q = (1/R)√(L/C) = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR). A high Q means the circuit responds sharply to frequencies near resonance (narrow bandwidth) — useful in radio tuning. A low Q means broader but flatter resonance. Q also equals the ratio of energy stored to energy lost per cycle.
